sourceRegistry.title: Claude Frontier Academy
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Anthropic announced Claude Frontier Academy with a $100 million commitment, aiming to train 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027. The target is not a completed result.
editorialCautions: Commitment is not money already spent
Goal is not number already trained

sourceRegistry.title: Gemini 4 Argon
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Google announced Gemini 4 Argon on 30 September. Its stated uses include programming. Initial access is limited to selected cyber defenders; broader access is planned after testing.
editorialCautions: Do not imply unrestricted public availability
Performance assertions are company claims
Original page says one million token output limit; do not confuse it with context window

sourceRegistry.title: GPT-6.1 Sol
sourceRegistry.factSummary: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol on 29 September for work including coding and documents. Announced standard API usage prices are $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, not subscriptions.
editorialCautions: API usage prices are not subscription prices
Near-Astra performance is an OpenAI evaluation claim
Availability can change; launch had Work/Codex/API availability, not Chat

sourceRegistry.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Anthropic announced Sonnet 5.5 for everyday work. It reports faster output and lower task costs than Sonnet 5. Standard input and output token prices are unchanged; claimed savings rely on using fewer tokens.
editorialCautions: Attribute speed and task-cost comparisons to Anthropic tests.
Do not turn up to 30% task savings into a 30% reduction in token price.

sourceRegistry.title: Claude Opus 5.5
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Anthropic announced Opus 5.5 for complex work, with standard API prices of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Performance and typical-workload savings are company-reported comparisons.
editorialCautions: Treat performance and 40% typical-workload cost reduction as company claims.
Distinguish token price, workload cost and subscription.

sourceRegistry.title: Skills in Gemini
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Google announced reusable custom instructions called skills in Gemini chat. Skills can reuse instructions and reference files. The announcement sets out a later transition from Gems with account-dependent schedules.
editorialCautions: Rollout and migration timing are time-sensitive; keep as announcement-dated facts.
Do not promise specific account availability.
Avoid teaching a UI invocation symbol as a permanent fact.

sourceRegistry.title: Report on a model distillation campaign
sourceRegistry.factSummary: OpenAI reports disrupting attempts to extract protected model reasoning. It describes technical controls, account enforcement and partner coordination, with investigations continuing. These are attributed security-report claims, not independently verified findings.
editorialCautions: Keep report and attribution claims explicitly attributed to OpenAI.
Do not claim that attackers directly accessed stored user conversations; the source says otherwise.
The beginner lesson should explain checking information and permission, not attack procedures.

sourceRegistry.title: Data Agent Kit general availability
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Google Cloud announced Data Agent Kit general availability, connecting coding agents with data services using the user’s permissions. The kit is described as free; underlying cloud use may still have charges.
editorialCautions: Free kit does not establish that underlying cloud usage is free.
Do not imply connection overrides permissions.

sourceRegistry.title: Early research on an enzyme system
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Anthropic reports that Claude helped identify an enzyme system associated with repeated DNA sequences. Human scientists performed laboratory work. The system’s function remains under investigation; this is early research, not a treatment.
editorialCautions: Early research is not an approved treatment or established medical breakthrough.
Attribute discovery account to Anthropic.
Keep technical terms recognition-only for beginners.

sourceRegistry.title: Introducing dots
sourceRegistry.factSummary: OpenAI introduced dots as proactive assistants working with a cloud computer and connected apps. The announcement describes user controls and approval boundaries. Its initial rollout was limited to specified paid plans and eligible markets.
editorialCautions: Do not promise availability to every account.
Do not equate autonomy with unlimited permission.
Use this as a dated product-news story, not a statement that every advertised feature is available in the current app.

sourceRegistry.title: Claude Frontier Academy program
sourceRegistry.factSummary: The official program page describes practical training, assessment and a 12-week residency on a real project. It gives a goal of 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027.
editorialCautions: Undated program page; do not invent a publication date.

sourceRegistry.title: Google September 2026 AI recap
sourceRegistry.factSummary: Google’s recap describes Gemini 4 Argon’s coding uses and staged access through Fairwind. The recap date is not the model’s original launch date.
editorialCautions: Use 30 September for the original Argon announcement.

sourceRegistry.title: GPT-6.1 Sol API model reference
sourceRegistry.factSummary: The model reference confirms standard usage-based pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
editorialCautions: Live reference; prices may change. Standard rates have conditions and are not a subscription quote.

lessons.title: New models and new training
lessons.subtitle: Three real AI stories with beginner language support
objectives: Recognise twelve useful Egyptian Arabic items
Read three short news passages with transliteration and English
Use this is, adjective agreement and a simple negative
Separate announced facts from imagined practice

Masculine. It can mean a training program or a software program; the context decides.

Learn it as one useful chunk today. This is not a full verb-conjugation lesson.
Learn the whole chunk. Egyptian everyday present forms often begin with a b sound; do not try to derive every verb from this example.

In today’s pattern, put it before the adjective or noun you negate. Other negatives need other patterns.

concepts.title: No separate is in these present-time sentences
concepts.explanation: For today’s simple statements identifying something or describing it now, Egyptian Arabic normally puts the parts together without a separate present-tense word for is. Read the whole sentence in natural English with is. This is a narrow first pattern, not a rule that Arabic never has a verb meaning be.
concepts.scope: Only present identity and adjective sentences are taught here. Past or future be, existence, location, and full person patterns are outside today’s lesson. Do not insert an English-style is word.

concepts.title: Two forms of this, and a small adjective change
concepts.explanation: Nouns have grammatical gender. A model or program is masculine here; company is feminine. Use da for the masculine pattern and dee for the feminine pattern. An adjective describing a feminine noun often has an added -a sound. Learn the two new forms as a pair today.
concepts.scope: These are simple this is ... sentences, not the separate pattern meaning this particular model. Do not memorize a complete gender system today.

concepts.title: A small negative: not
concepts.explanation: In these present descriptions, put mesh before the adjective. You can also use it before the noun in a simple identity statement. It negates that description or identity. This does not teach the full system for negating verbs.
concepts.scope: Do not make a general negative-verb rule from mesh. Treat the final Google news sentence as a recognition-only chunk.

metadata.title: Day 1: New models, new training
metadata.purpose: Read a few real AI-news ideas in everyday Egyptian Arabic, then build a handful of short sentences. This is guided exposure and first practice, not a claim of mastery.
metadata.startHere: You do not need to know the Arabic alphabet yet. Read the Latin line aloud first, then look at the matching Arabic. Choose a comfortable pace. Use the English gloss whenever you need it.
metadata.scope: Twelve focus items; three short readings. Harder news expressions are recognition-only today. Do not memorize every word in the news.
metadata.editorialPolicy: The readings are simplified teaching paraphrases of the linked company announcements, not quotations. Company-reported capabilities are attributed in the English context. Publication dates are not fabricated lesson dates. Fictional drills and the optional dialogue do not describe actual prices or availability.
metadata.accessibility: Arabic text should be displayed right-to-left; transliteration and English left-to-right, on separate lines. Offer an English-gloss toggle. In exercises, reveal stored glosses after answering so they do not give away the answer.
metadata.assessmentPolicy: Give explanations and allow retries. Accept Latin transliteration if the learner cannot type Arabic. Treat the result as today’s practice, not certification or proof of fluency.
metadata.progressPolicy: All learning records start unattempted and not_exposed. Authoring, rendering, and validating this content do not record learner exposure or performance. Only a real learner interaction may create an exposure or attempt event.
metadata.exerciseVocabularyPolicy: Words that appear only in recognition-only news glosses, factual-answer choices, or distractors are not additional focus targets. Full Arabic, transliteration, and English data are stored for every answer option, token, and canonical answer. The renderer can show only the relevant side before an answer.

transliteration.description: A practical pronunciation aid, not a formal transliteration standard. Egyptian pronunciation varies between speakers. The spellings here are consistent within this lesson; small vowel variations are acceptable.
rules: Short a, e, i, o, u are approximate vowels. Double aa, ee, oo mark a longer vowel: hold it a little longer.
sh is like sh in ship. kh is the rough sound in Scottish loch. gh is its voiced counterpart; neither is an English g.
g represents the usual Egyptian pronunciation of the Arabic letter jeem, as in English go.
ʿ marks the Arabic ayin, a voiced throat sound with no exact English equivalent. Try a gentle throat constriction; do not let it stop you speaking.
ʾ marks a glottal stop, the catch between the two parts of uh-oh. It commonly represents qaaf in these Egyptian words, but not every Egyptian word with qaaf is pronounced this way.
h is a beginner approximation for both Arabic h sounds in this lesson. It does not mean that the two Arabic consonants are identical.
el- means the. It sometimes blends into the following consonant: esh-, et-, and en-. These spellings show the spoken sound.
The small word fee means in. In a connected phrase it can join the following article, as fel- or fesh-.

Brand and product names are the one deliberate exception: their familiar official Latin spellings are retained in the pronunciation line. Digits remain digits. They are names to recognize, not new Arabic spelling targets.

examples.english: can / is able to, in the news sentence
with work / at work, depending on context

answerTolerance.specialCharacters: Accept 3 for ʿ and 2 or an apostrophe for ʾ. A learner may omit these unfamiliar symbols on Day 1 if the intended word is clear. Explain the sound gently instead of marking an otherwise correct sentence wrong.
answerTolerance.feedback: Do not silently treat a feminine demonstrative with a masculine noun as correct. Explain the agreement and allow another try. Flexible spelling is different from changing the grammar.
answerTolerance.arabicInput: Ignore punctuation, optional vowel marks, tatweel, and harmless spacing differences. Accept Arabic or Western digits where relevant. Keep lexical and gender differences meaningful; they are not just spelling variations.
answerTolerance.latinInput: Ignore capitalization, punctuation, hyphens, and repeated spaces. Accept common e/i vowel choices, da/dah, dee/di, mesh/mish, gedeed/gedid/gadid, sherka/shirka, rekhees/rikhees/rakhis, moodeel/model, and common article spellings el-/il-/al-. concepts.title: Match the adjective to the noun
concepts.explanation: In these present-tense descriptions there is no separate word for is. A masculine noun takes the masculine adjective; a feminine noun takes its feminine form, often ending in -a. The tool and company words in this lesson are feminine. The model and training words are masculine. Learn the slow pair separately because its pronunciation changes. An indefinite describing adjective follows its noun. Do not add the feminine ending to every adjective mechanically.

optionalSourceRetrieval.instruction: Open one linked canonical source record. State its main point and one caution in English. This is supported source reading, not extra vocabulary to memorize.

assessmentRules.transliterationVariations: Accept reasonable vowel and glottal-stop spelling variants after semantic review; show the course spelling as feedback.
assessmentRules.acceptedPronunciationVariants: Meaning-preserving Cairo vowel variants in learner transliteration are accepted after semantic review, including asʾila/asʾela and muhandis/mohandes. Show the canonical course form without claiming a pronunciation or script-spelling failure.

concepts.title: Ask about things and people
concepts.explanation: Use the what-question for a thing, meaning or activity; use the who-question for a person. In a basic identity question, put the demonstrative first and the question word last. When asking who does an action, the who-word can come first. Learn these whole frames rather than translating English word order. The person-question does not require a present-tense is.

concepts.title: Say what you do every day
concepts.explanation: For the first-person habitual actions taught here, learn the whole verb chunks: I work, I learn and I use. Their initial b sound marks this ordinary present/habitual use. The explicit I pronoun can be included for clarity. These first-person verbs do not change with the speaker’s gender, but an occupational noun does. Do not extrapolate a full conjugation from one verb; vowel patterns differ. Every day naturally follows the action.

concepts.title: Say who reads or writes what
concepts.explanation: Use subject, verb, then object in these neutral beginner sentences. The object needs no special noun ending. The article makes the object definite: the document versus a document. Learn reads and writes as masculine third-person chunks today. The short vowel is part of the whole chunk, not an English auxiliary. To change who does the action, do not merely swap a male subject for a female subject and leave the verb unchanged.

concepts.title: Ask and give a small price
concepts.explanation: Learn one, two and ten as standalone numbers, then use the fixed price frames below. One follows a counted noun and has a feminine partner. Two objects are often expressed with a dual noun, but this lesson does not ask you to build that form. For prices, practise the colloquial two-pound and ten-pound chunks exactly as given. Free of charge is a price statement, while inexpensive is a judgment; they do not mean the same thing. Fictional pound prices are unrelated to real API token rates.

concepts.title: Ask where; say what is there
concepts.explanation: To locate a known item, name it and add the where-question, or name it and give here or there. There is no separate is in these location frames. To introduce the existence of something, use the there-is chunk before an indefinite noun. Its English translation can be there is or there are depending on the following phrase. Do not confuse there-is with the place word there. These are distinct expressions.

concepts.title: Learn a few plurals as pairs
concepts.explanation: Learn these plural nouns as vocabulary pairs: file/files, tool/tools and question/questions. Their shapes differ, so adding one ending to every noun will not work. The people word is already plural in meaning. Many often follows the plural noun in the beginner frames here; a few comes before the noun and its final sound links as -it. A few is an approximate small amount, not an exact count, and the same word can mean some or a little in other contexts. Team is a singular collective noun in the model sentence.

optionalSourceRetrieval.instruction: Open one linked canonical source record. State its main point and one caution in English. This is supported source reading, not extra vocabulary to memorize.
optionalSourceRetrieval.answerRule: Use the canonical facts and cautions only. Do not infer account access, clinical outcomes, completed targets or unlimited permission.

assessmentRules.transliterationVariations: Accept reasonable vowel and glottal-stop spelling variants after semantic review; show the course spelling as feedback.
assessmentRules.acceptedPronunciationVariants: Meaning-preserving Cairo vowel variants in learner transliteration are accepted after semantic review, including asʾila/asʾela and muhandis/mohandes. Show the canonical course form without claiming a pronunciation or script-spelling failure.

concepts.title: Make one clear, polite request
concepts.explanation: Learn read, write and say as a few request chunks, not a complete command paradigm. The basic forms here address one man; the feminine forms have an added -i sound. Please also changes pronunciation with the addressee’s gender even though the ordinary unvowelled spelling is the same. Again usually follows the requested action. For a short answer, the adjective must match the feminine answer noun. Requests are practice utterances, not commands to a real service.

concepts.title: Say what you need — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Use aayiz (male speaker) or aayza (female speaker) for want; mihtaag or mihtaaga for need. These describe the speaker, so their endings do not agree with the object wanted. A woman wanting a masculine noun still uses aayza. Put a noun or a simple verb after the chunk. No present-tense 'am' is added. Learn aayiz at'allim as a whole phrase: I want to learn.

concepts.title: Compare two choices — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Learn arkhas (cheaper), asra' (faster) and ahsan (better) as whole comparative words. Follow with min for than: da asra' min da. These comparative frames do not need the ordinary feminine -a ending. Mikhtilif/mokhtalfa is an ordinary adjective meaning different, not a comparative. Compare a stated property, not a model's quality on every possible task.

concepts.title: Check before using — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Mumkin introduces a practical permission question: mumkin astakhdim da? Can I use this? The following first-person verb has no habitual b-prefix here. Momkin is a common transliteration variant accepted alongside mumkin. An affirmative permission answer is different from a claim that software is safe. Keep izn (permission) and aamin (safe) separate.

transliterationGuide.consonants: sh, kh, gh; g for Egyptian jeem; ʿ for ain; ʾ for a glottal stop, including usual Egyptian qaf. h approximates both Arabic h consonants.
transliterationGuide.article: el-; sound assimilation before appropriate consonants appears as esh-, et-, or en-. Egyptian g in el-gomla and el-gaay does not trigger assimilation.
transliterationGuide.acceptedInput: Variants mish/mesh, di/dee, il-/el- and aayiz/ʿaayiz are valid transliteration inputs; spelling mastery is separate.
transliterationGuide.mode: No audio. Arabic script remains authoritative.

concepts.explanation: With ish-shirka (the company), learn a'lanit (announced) and nazzilit (released). The feminine ending belongs to the company as grammatical subject. Do not add habitual bi- to these completed past forms. Imbaarih means yesterday relative to the speaker. A publication date is safer than calling an old story yesterday's news.

concepts.title: Say when something happens — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Imta asks when, while feen asks where. Learn el-usbooʿ da (this week), ish-shahr da (this month), and baʿdeen (later) as time chunks. In colloquial Egyptian the demonstrative follows the noun here. A time phrase does not prove that a planned event happened. Use past a'lanit only for a completed announcement.

concepts.title: Plans are different from results — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Use ha- with a small set of familiar verbs: ha'ra, I will read; haktib, I will write; hat'allim, I will learn. This replaces the habitual b-prefix; do not stack both prefixes. The spelling commonly joins ح to the verb. Il-usbooʿ el-gaay means next week. Future wording reports an intention or expectation, not a completed result or a guarantee. The future prefix can be written with حـ or هـ in colloquial spelling; this lesson uses هـ in its sentence examples.

concepts.title: A scientist checks a result — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Compare biyraagi' (checks/is checking) with raaga' (checked), using a male researcher as the subject. Place the object after the verb: il-baahis biyraagi' in-nateega. The feminine result noun does not make the male subject's verb feminine. Mish ma'ruuf means unknown with a masculine subject; mish ma'ruufa with a feminine one. Do not infer medical usefulness from an early laboratory result.

concepts.title: Report what a company says — Egyptian sentence pattern
concepts.explanation: Use biy'uul with a male person and bit'uul with ish-shirka (the company). Hasab comes before the named source. Yimkin marks maybe; lissa mish works with nonverbal descriptions: lissa mish waadih, not clear yet. With verbs, negation may instead wrap ma-...-sh around the verb; do not generalise lissa mish to every construction. Reporting words and source names preserve uncertainty.

concepts.title: Retrieve attribution, descriptive negation and temporal distinctions
concepts.explanation: Retrieve attribution without turning it into proof. Hasab (according to) names the source. Mesh negates a description, while lissa mesh means not yet before that description. To say an action has not happened yet, a different negative pattern is used; this is recognition-only, not a production target today. Kamaan means also; bass between two clauses means but. Use short familiar clauses and keep the uncertainty word when retelling.

concepts.title: Sequence markers with known verbs
concepts.explanation: Use el-awwal (first) and baʿdeen (then) to join familiar actions. Baʿd (after) and ʾabl (before) come before their noun phrase, unlike Hungarian postpositions. Baʿdeen can also mean later; the situation supplies the exact time. The b-prefix marks a present routine in these examples. The past forms aʿlanit and nazzilit have a feminine subject because company is feminine. Treat them as learned chunks, not a new full conjugation table.

concepts.title: If-conditions with a simple present or future response; no counterfactual lesson
concepts.explanation: Law introduces a possible condition. The response may use ha- for a future action: law ... hagarrab means if ... I will try. A description such as available is negated with mesh; it does not need the verbal ma-...-sh pattern. Imta asks when. Baʿd usbooʿ means in a week in this future setting; baʿdeen simply means later. do not infer a precise date from it. These are realistic conditions, not unreal past or counterfactual constructions.

concepts.title: I do not understand, with speaker-gender agreement; explanation requests
concepts.explanation: A male speaker says ana mesh faahim; a female speaker says ana mesh faahma. These describe a state of understanding. For a request to one man, use ishrah; to one woman, ishrahi. Min fadlak and min fadlik likewise depend on the addressee, not the speaker. Birraaha can mean slowly or gently in context. Mathematically literal word-by-word translations are less useful than this natural request: explain it to me slowly. Use a clear example to repair understanding. For the supported reconstruction, learn babuss ʿala as one chunk meaning I look at. You may keep that chunk visible while producing the rest of the sentence.

concepts.title: Only, all and some in clear examples; distinguish only from but
concepts.explanation: Bass has two jobs. Between contrasting clauses it means but; after a limited item it can mean only: el-malaff da bass means only this file. Kull means all or every. Baʿd plus a definite plural gives some of the group; it is used in educated speech, while shwayyit is another everyday option meaning some/a few. Mesh kull means not all, which is different from none. Review agreement with feminine nateega and masculine ikhtibaar. scope words matter more than a dramatic headline.

concepts.title: In my opinion and why, with polite agreement chunks
concepts.explanation: Fi raʾyi marks your opinion. Ana mowaafeʾ and ana mesh mowaafeʾ are agreement chunks for a male speaker; a female speaker uses mowaafʾa. Leeh asks why and ʿashaan supplies a reason. Agreeing with a person is not the same as independently verifying their claim. In conversation, disagree with a specific statement and give a reason. Keep lissa mesh before a descriptive predicate; do not omit lissa when the point is that evidence is not sufficient yet.

concepts.title: Combine known sentence patterns; no new grammar
concepts.explanation: Combine familiar patterns rather than adding a new conjugation. A ʿinwaan is a headline or title; a haʾeeʾa is a fact; an iddiʿaaʾ is a claim or allegation; a daleel is evidence. In everyday speech you can also say the company says rather than using the more formal noun claim. The noun alone does not show whether something is true or false. Put ʾabl and baʿd before a noun, or use a supported before-I-answer chunk. Keep source and opinion markers when combining sentences.

readings.instruction: Az Anthropic egy cég means ‘Anthropic is a company’. There is no separate word for ‘is’ in this sentence. In segít tanulni, tanulni means ‘to learn’.

readings.title: A new model with limited access
readings.instruction: In egy új modell, új comes before the noun: ‘a new model’. In A modell új, it comes after: ‘The model is new’.

concepts.title: This is something
concepts.explanation: In this kind of present-tense singular third-person identity sentence, Hungarian has no separate word for 'is'. This is not a general rule for all persons, existence or location.

concepts.title: The thing is new
concepts.explanation: A singular third-person subject can be described by an adjective without a separate 'is'. An adjective before a noun describes that noun; after the subject it says what the subject is like in this basic pattern.

concepts.title: A or an and the
concepts.explanation: Egy can mean a/an. A and az mean the. Use a before a consonant sound and az before a vowel sound. Look at the next spoken word.

concepts.title: A simple negative
concepts.explanation: In this basic adjective sentence, nem goes before the adjective.

concepts.title: An action verb stays
concepts.explanation: Tanul is an action verb and stays in the sentence. Depending on context, tanul means learns or is learning. You do not need the whole conjugation table today.

concepts.title: Read a news claim carefully
concepts.explanation: Distinguish a future target, limited availability and a usage price.

concepts.title: Attributive versus predicate adjectives in singular frames
concepts.explanation: An adjective directly before a singular noun describes it: egy gyors modell, a fast model. In A modell gyors, the adjective is the predicate: the model is fast. These third-person present descriptions omit is. Hungarian has no grammatical masculine/feminine agreement, so gyors stays gyors with modell, cég or képzés. The article follows the sound of the next word: a modell but az új modell. Today use singular nouns only.

concepts.title: Mi and ki questions; familiar action verbs
concepts.explanation: Mi asks what; ki asks who. Mi ez? means What is this? Ki segít? asks which person helps. A question with an action verb keeps the verb: Mi segít? can ask what helps. Do not add van to Mi ez? For today's supported dialogue, learn Mit csinál? (What does he/she/it do?) as a complete chunk: mit is the object form of mi, but a full case system is not today's goal.

concepts.title: First person present as a few high-value chunks
concepts.explanation: Hungarian marks the subject on the verb. Learn tanulok (I learn/study), dolgozom (I work), and használok (I use) as three complete present-tense chunks. Én means I and can be omitted when the verb makes the person clear. In an identity sentence about yourself, keep vagyok: Én mérnök vagyok. Compare Anna mérnök, with no is. The adverb mindennap means every day and is written as one word. The separate phrase minden nap can also mean every/each day; do not assume the one-word form is the only possible construction. Today practise the adverb mindennap before or after the simple clause.

concepts.title: Recognition and limited production of accusative -t with known nouns
concepts.explanation: The object is what someone reads, writes or uses. In today’s indefinite-object chunks, Hungarian marks it with -t, sometimes adding a linking vowel: fájl → fájlt; dokumentum → dokumentumot; eszköz → eszközt. Learn these three whole forms rather than guessing every noun. A diák egy fájlt olvas means The student reads a file. A fájl új describes the file itself, so fájl has no object ending. Definite-object verb conjugation is deliberately postponed.

concepts.title: Cardinal numbers with singular nouns; price chunks
concepts.explanation: After a cardinal number, Hungarian normally uses a singular noun: egy fájl, két fájl, tíz fájl. Do not add plural -k simply because the number is greater than one. Use két directly before a noun and kettő as the number by itself in this beginner pattern. Ingyenes means free of charge, while olcsó means inexpensive: they are not synonyms. Mennyibe kerül? is your reusable price question. For API prices, always retain the unit: per million input or output tokens.

concepts.title: Hol and selected -ban/-ben location chunks; van in location contrasted with description
concepts.explanation: Descriptions and locations behave differently. A számítógép új means The computer is new, with no is. A számítógép itt van means The computer is here and requires van in this full location sentence. Ask Hol van a fájl? Learn a few location chunks: a mappában (in the folder), a dokumentumban (in the document), a képzésben (in the training). The -ban/-ben endings mean in; their vowel choice follows vowel harmony. Practise the supplied chunks rather than deriving all possible forms.

concepts.title: Basic noun plurals; quantities often followed by singular noun
concepts.explanation: Without a number or quantity word, learn common plural forms: modell → modellek, eszköz → eszközök, ember → emberek. The endings differ, so store each complete form. After két, sok or kevés, keep a singular noun: két eszköz, sok ember, kevés modell. A csapat is singular even though it contains several people. In a simple plural adjective statement, both noun and predicate adjective are plural: A modellek gyorsak. An adjective directly before a plural noun stays unmarked: gyors modellek. In location statements, an unquantified plural needs vannak: Az emberek itt vannak (The people are here). After sok or kevés, the grammatical singular uses van: Sok ember van itt (Many people are here). Learn the contrast without a full conjugation table.

concepts.title: Polite request chunks, not full imperative paradigm
concepts.explanation: Learn a small formal-polite request set as complete chunks: Kérem, írjon! (Please write!), Kérem, olvassa el! (Please read it!), and Még egyszer, kérem (Once more, please). Újra also means again, as in A diák újra olvas (The student reads again). We are not deriving the whole Hungarian imperative today. For a short answer, use Kérem, írjon egy rövid választ! The object form of válasz is választ. A clear answer is világos; in this context that means understandable, not necessarily bright. These requests can address a helper politely; the fictional scenes do not prescribe an actual AI interface.

concepts.title: Szeretnék and kell as bounded chunks
concepts.explanation: Use szeretnék + infinitive for I would like to do something: szeretnék tanulni. With a thing, learn the whole object chunk: egy eszközt szeretnék. Kell expresses necessity: Idő kell = Time is needed / I need time in context. It is not a conjugated equivalent of English I need. Do not put an object -t on idő in this frame. Contrast a polite wish with a need; Hungarian does not mark the speaker's gender.

concepts.explanation: Learn olcsó → olcsóbb, gyors → gyorsabb, jó → jobb. Do not build the irregular jobb mechanically. The comparison target follows mint: Ez olcsóbb, mint az. In these singular adjective sentences there is no van. Más means different/another here, not more. Our comparisons of unnamed classroom tools are imagined; they do not establish a real model ranking.

concepts.title: Tud plus infinitive in limited ability frames
concepts.explanation: Tud + infinitive expresses ability: tud olvasni, can read. In Tudok egy fájlt olvasni, tudok marks I and olvasni stays infinitive. Do not add a second finite verb. Ability does not automatically mean authorization; ask Van engedély? separately. Learn Ellenőrizd a forrást, Check the source, as a bounded instruction, not a whole imperative paradigm. Elolvashatok egy fájlt? is a supported permission-request chunk, distinct from the ability frame tudok olvasni.

concepts.title: Mikor and time expressions; past versus present context
concepts.explanation: Mikor asks when; hol asks where. Learn ezen a héten (this week), ebben a hónapban (this month) and később (later) as entire time chunks. They do not determine tense by themselves: a completed announcement still needs a past form. Hét means week here, but also seven in other contexts. Keep later distinct from an exact promised date.

concepts.title: Fog plus infinitive in fixed examples; date-relative caution
concepts.explanation: Use fog + infinitive for a limited future frame: A csapat tanulni fog. With I, use fogok: Tanulni fogok. concepts.title: Retrieve attribution and temporal distinctions
concepts.explanation: Retrieve the difference between attribution and opinion: X szerint means according to X; szerintem marks your own opinion. Azt mondja introduces what someone says. Még nem means not yet and does not mean never. In a description, nem goes before the adjective; do not insert van into a third-person adjective sentence. Is normally follows the word it adds. Today introduces no new grammar. Read each pair, cover the Hungarian, then reconstruct only the short clause you can support.

concepts.title: Sequence markers with known verbs
concepts.explanation: Use először and aztán to order clauses with verbs you already know. Után and előtt follow the noun phrase: a munka után is after work; a teszt előtt is before the test. Do not place them before the noun as in English. Keep tense fixed within a small retelling: present for a routine, familiar past chunks for yesterday's fictional bulletin. Recognise ellenőrzöm as I check it and elolvasom as I read it through; the entire definite-conjugation system is not a production target.

concepts.title: Ha with a present-tense condition; no full conditional mood
concepts.explanation: Ha introduces a real or possible condition. Use familiar present-tense verbs in both halves; this is not the Hungarian conditional mood. Ha nem elérhető, később próbálom means if it is not available, I will try it later in this context. A comma separates the clauses. Mikor asks when; később is deliberately vague. A hét and a hónap mean the week and the month, while one week is egy hét. Keep uncertainty rather than inventing a date.

concepts.title: Jobban szeretem as a chunk and sufficient adjective practice
concepts.explanation: Jobban szeretem is a useful first-person chunk meaning I prefer. Learn the object with it: az egyszerű eszközt, the simple tool. Elég may mean enough by itself or stand before a quantity. Drága is expensive, while egyszerű is simple; these are judgments about the imagined tools, not claims about named products. Review a future chunk with fog plus infinitive, without memorising its entire paradigm. A következő feladat means the next task; the adjective stays before the noun.

concepts.title: Nem értem and please-explain chunks
concepts.explanation: Nem értem is a compact and useful repair phrase: I do not understand. Kérlek, magyarázd el means please explain it to someone you address informally. The verb and el separate in this imperative chunk; learn the whole request. Lassan is the adverb slowly, not the adjective slow. Egy példa is the subject form, but kérek egy példát uses an object form. Both are the same vocabulary family. Add mert for a reason and de for a contrast, keeping the request short.

concepts.title: Quantifier contrasts and explicit scope
concepts.explanation: Minden, néhány and numerals normally take singular nouns: minden fájl, néhány kutató, két teszt. Csak narrows the scope of the phrase that follows. Compare only this file with all files; neither implies anything about every user's access. In a negative sentence not every is different from no: nem minden fájl means not every file. Learn the contrast directly rather than building a large quantifier table. Keep teszt and eredmény separate: a test is a procedure, a result is what it produces.

concepts.title: Szerintem and miért conversation frames
concepts.explanation: Szerintem introduces your own view; Anna szerint attributes a view to Anna. Neither is evidence by itself. Miért asks why and mert gives a reason. Egyetértek is I agree, but the negative chunk is nem értek egyet: the verbal prefix separates in this learned pattern. Do not mechanically put nem before the whole positive word. A polite disagreement can name the particular point: I agree about the date, but not the conclusion. Today keep your production to one judgment and one reason.

concepts.title: Mixed retrieval focused on weakest concepts
concepts.explanation: This is retrieval, not a new paradigm. First try the three dialogue functions without a word bank: ask for explanation, express an opinion, and ask why. You can simplify a long sentence into two short ones and retain its meaning. Score independent production separately from reconstructed answers after seeing the model.

concepts.title: Combine known sentence patterns; no new grammar
concepts.explanation: No new grammar today. Combine familiar description, sequence and object chunks while introducing four news-literacy nouns. Cím can be a headline or title. Állítás is a claim, whether true or false; calling something a claim does not establish that it is false. Bizonyíték is evidence, and tény is a fact. Practise the object form in elolvasom a címet. Keep the noun forms supported; the main task is separating a title, a claim, and the evidence offered for it.

concepts.title: Capstone using known forms and source checking
concepts.explanation: This capstone combines known forms. Choose one source card, keep its date, and write a very short brief with a headline, one attributed statement and one limit. You may use two simple sentences instead of one long clause. Use ha for a condition, szerintem for your opinion and szerint for another source's position. Agreeing is not proof, and a well-written sentence is not proof that a product claim is true.

conceptRegistry.title: This is something
conceptRegistry.explanation: In this kind of present-tense singular third-person identity sentence, Hungarian has no separate word for 'is'. This is not a general rule for all persons, existence or location.

conceptRegistry.title: The thing is new
conceptRegistry.explanation: A singular third-person subject can be described by an adjective without a separate 'is'. An adjective before a noun describes that noun; after the subject it says what the subject is like in this basic pattern.

conceptRegistry.title: A or an and the
conceptRegistry.explanation: Egy can mean a/an. A and az mean the. Use a before a consonant sound and az before a vowel sound. Look at the next spoken word.

conceptRegistry.title: A simple negative
conceptRegistry.explanation: In this basic adjective sentence, nem goes before the adjective.

conceptRegistry.title: An action verb stays
conceptRegistry.explanation: Tanul is an action verb and stays in the sentence. Depending on context, tanul means learns or is learning. You do not need the whole conjugation table today.

conceptRegistry.title: Read a news claim carefully
conceptRegistry.explanation: Distinguish a future target, limited availability and a usage price. This reading-comprehension concept is separate from Hungarian grammar mastery.

conceptRegistry.title: No separate is in these present-time sentences
conceptRegistry.explanation: For today’s simple statements identifying something or describing it now, Egyptian Arabic normally puts the parts together without a separate present-tense word for is. Read the whole sentence in natural English with is. This is a narrow first pattern, not a rule that Arabic never has a verb meaning be.

conceptRegistry.title: Two forms of this, and a small adjective change
conceptRegistry.explanation: Nouns have grammatical gender. A model or program is masculine here; company is feminine. Use da for the masculine pattern and dee for the feminine pattern. An adjective describing a feminine noun often has an added -a sound. Learn the two new forms as a pair today.

conceptRegistry.title: A small negative: not
conceptRegistry.explanation: In these present descriptions, put mesh before the adjective. You can also use it before the noun in a simple identity statement. It negates that description or identity. This does not teach the full system for negating verbs.

conceptRegistry.title: Understand a dated source claim
conceptRegistry.explanation: Distinguish the product or program named in a source from invented language practice. This comprehension concept does not prove Arabic grammar mastery.

conceptRegistry.title: Match the adjective to the noun
conceptRegistry.explanation: In these present-tense descriptions there is no separate word for is. A masculine noun takes the masculine adjective; a feminine noun takes its feminine form, often ending in -a. The tool and company words in this lesson are feminine. The model and training words are masculine. Learn the slow pair separately because its pronunciation changes. An indefinite describing adjective follows its noun. Do not add the feminine ending to every adjective mechanically.

conceptRegistry.title: Ask about things and people
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use the what-question for a thing, meaning or activity; use the who-question for a person. In a basic identity question, put the demonstrative first and the question word last. When asking who does an action, the who-word can come first. Learn these whole frames rather than translating English word order. The person-question does not require a present-tense is.

conceptRegistry.title: Say what you do every day
conceptRegistry.explanation: For the first-person habitual actions taught here, learn the whole verb chunks: I work, I learn and I use. Their initial b sound marks this ordinary present/habitual use. The explicit I pronoun can be included for clarity. These first-person verbs do not change with the speaker’s gender, but an occupational noun does. Do not extrapolate a full conjugation from one verb; vowel patterns differ. Every day naturally follows the action.

conceptRegistry.title: Say who reads or writes what
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use subject, verb, then object in these neutral beginner sentences. The object needs no special noun ending. The article makes the object definite: the document versus a document. Learn reads and writes as masculine third-person chunks today. The short vowel is part of the whole chunk, not an English auxiliary. To change who does the action, do not merely swap a male subject for a female subject and leave the verb unchanged.

conceptRegistry.title: Ask and give a small price
conceptRegistry.explanation: Learn one, two and ten as standalone numbers, then use the fixed price frames below. One follows a counted noun and has a feminine partner. Two objects are often expressed with a dual noun, but this lesson does not ask you to build that form. For prices, practise the colloquial two-pound and ten-pound chunks exactly as given. Free of charge is a price statement, while inexpensive is a judgment; they do not mean the same thing. Fictional pound prices are unrelated to real API token rates.

conceptRegistry.title: Retrieve the first six days
conceptRegistry.explanation: This is consolidation, with no new focus items. First identify the noun’s gender, then choose the demonstrative and adjective. For people use the who-question; for things use the what-question. Retrieve whole first-person action chunks and familiar price chunks. If you cannot recall a word, mark the attempt before opening a hint. Reading the correct form afterward is exposure, not successful independent recall.

conceptRegistry.title: Ask where; say what is there
conceptRegistry.explanation: To locate a known item, name it and add the where-question, or name it and give here or there. There is no separate is in these location frames. To introduce the existence of something, use the there-is chunk before an indefinite noun. Its English translation can be there is or there are depending on the following phrase. Do not confuse there-is with the place word there. These are distinct expressions.

conceptRegistry.title: Learn a few plurals as pairs
conceptRegistry.explanation: Learn these plural nouns as vocabulary pairs: file/files, tool/tools and question/questions. Their shapes differ, so adding one ending to every noun will not work. The people word is already plural in meaning. Many often follows the plural noun in the beginner frames here; a few comes before the noun and its final sound links as -it. A few is an approximate small amount, not an exact count, and the same word can mean some or a little in other contexts. Team is a singular collective noun in the model sentence.

conceptRegistry.title: Make one clear, polite request
conceptRegistry.explanation: Learn read, write and say as a few request chunks, not a complete command paradigm. The basic forms here address one man; the feminine forms have an added -i sound. Please also changes pronunciation with the addressee’s gender even though the ordinary unvowelled spelling is the same. Again usually follows the requested action. For a short answer, the adjective must match the feminine answer noun. Requests are practice utterances, not commands to a real service.

conceptRegistry.title: Attributive versus predicate adjectives in singular frames
conceptRegistry.explanation: An adjective directly before a singular noun describes it: egy gyors modell, a fast model. In A modell gyors, the adjective is the predicate: the model is fast. These third-person present descriptions omit is. Hungarian has no grammatical masculine/feminine agreement, so gyors stays gyors with modell, cég or képzés. The article follows the sound of the next word: a modell but az új modell. Today use singular nouns only.

conceptRegistry.title: Mi and ki questions; familiar action verbs
conceptRegistry.explanation: Mi asks what; ki asks who. Mi ez? means What is this? Ki segít? asks which person helps. A question with an action verb keeps the verb: Mi segít? can ask what helps. Do not add van to Mi ez? For today's supported dialogue, learn Mit csinál? (What does he/she/it do?) as a complete chunk: mit is the object form of mi, but a full case system is not today's goal.

conceptRegistry.title: First person present as a few high-value chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: Hungarian marks the subject on the verb. Learn tanulok (I learn/study), dolgozom (I work), and használok (I use) as three complete present-tense chunks. Én means I and can be omitted when the verb makes the person clear. In an identity sentence about yourself, keep vagyok: Én mérnök vagyok. Compare Anna mérnök, with no is. The adverb mindennap means every day and is written as one word. The separate phrase minden nap can also mean every/each day; do not assume the one-word form is the only possible construction. Today practise the adverb mindennap before or after the simple clause.

conceptRegistry.title: Recognition and limited production of accusative -t with known nouns
conceptRegistry.explanation: The object is what someone reads, writes or uses. In today’s indefinite-object chunks, Hungarian marks it with -t, sometimes adding a linking vowel: fájl → fájlt; dokumentum → dokumentumot; eszköz → eszközt. Learn these three whole forms rather than guessing every noun. A diák egy fájlt olvas means The student reads a file. A fájl új describes the file itself, so fájl has no object ending. Definite-object verb conjugation is deliberately postponed.

conceptRegistry.title: Cardinal numbers with singular nouns; price chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: After a cardinal number, Hungarian normally uses a singular noun: egy fájl, két fájl, tíz fájl. Do not add plural -k simply because the number is greater than one. Use két directly before a noun and kettő as the number by itself in this beginner pattern. Ingyenes means free of charge, while olcsó means inexpensive: they are not synonyms. Mennyibe kerül? is your reusable price question. For API prices, always retain the unit: per million input or output tokens.

conceptRegistry.title: Retrieve identity, adjective, questions and object chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: This consolidation introduces no new focus vocabulary. Retrieve four patterns: Ez egy új eszköz (identity), Az eszköz hasznos (description), Mi ez? / Ki segít? (questions), and A diák egy fájlt olvas (a known object chunk). First-person identity still requires vagyok. Numbers still take singular nouns. Attempt from memory, use one hint if needed, then record that the answer was supported rather than independent.

conceptRegistry.title: Hol and selected -ban/-ben location chunks; van in location contrasted with description
conceptRegistry.explanation: Descriptions and locations behave differently. A számítógép új means The computer is new, with no is. A számítógép itt van means The computer is here and requires van in this full location sentence. Ask Hol van a fájl? Learn a few location chunks: a mappában (in the folder), a dokumentumban (in the document), a képzésben (in the training). The -ban/-ben endings mean in; their vowel choice follows vowel harmony. Practise the supplied chunks rather than deriving all possible forms.

conceptRegistry.title: Basic noun plurals; quantities often followed by singular noun
conceptRegistry.explanation: Without a number or quantity word, learn common plural forms: modell → modellek, eszköz → eszközök, ember → emberek. The endings differ, so store each complete form. After két, sok or kevés, keep a singular noun: két eszköz, sok ember, kevés modell. A csapat is singular even though it contains several people. In a simple plural adjective statement, both noun and predicate adjective are plural: A modellek gyorsak. An adjective directly before a plural noun stays unmarked: gyors modellek. In location statements, an unquantified plural needs vannak: Az emberek itt vannak (The people are here). After sok or kevés, the grammatical singular uses van: Sok ember van itt (Many people are here). Learn the contrast without a full conjugation table.

conceptRegistry.title: Polite request chunks, not full imperative paradigm
conceptRegistry.explanation: Learn a small formal-polite request set as complete chunks: Kérem, írjon! (Please write!), Kérem, olvassa el! (Please read it!), and Még egyszer, kérem (Once more, please). Újra also means again, as in A diák újra olvas (The student reads again). We are not deriving the whole Hungarian imperative today. For a short answer, use Kérem, írjon egy rövid választ! The object form of válasz is választ. A clear answer is világos; in this context that means understandable, not necessarily bright. These requests can address a helper politely; the fictional scenes do not prescribe an actual AI interface.

conceptRegistry.title: Say what you need — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use aayiz (male speaker) or aayza (female speaker) for want; mihtaag or mihtaaga for need. These describe the speaker, so their endings do not agree with the object wanted. A woman wanting a masculine noun still uses aayza. Put a noun or a simple verb after the chunk. No present-tense 'am' is added. Learn aayiz at'allim as a whole phrase: I want to learn.

conceptRegistry.title: Compare two choices — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Learn arkhas (cheaper), asra' (faster) and ahsan (better) as whole comparative words. Follow with min for than: da asra' min da. These comparative frames do not need the ordinary feminine -a ending. Mikhtilif/mokhtalfa is an ordinary adjective meaning different, not a comparative. Compare a stated property, not a model's quality on every possible task.

conceptRegistry.title: Check before using — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Mumkin introduces a practical permission question: mumkin astakhdim da? Can I use this? The following first-person verb has no habitual b-prefix here. Momkin is a common transliteration variant accepted alongside mumkin. An affirmative permission answer is different from a claim that software is safe. Keep izn (permission) and aamin (safe) separate.

conceptRegistry.title: Review and make a small choice — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Retrieve want/need agreement, zero-copula descriptions and mumkin permission questions. Choose aayiz/mihtaag for a male speaker, aayza/mihtaaga for a female speaker. Di adaa gedeeda uses a feminine noun and adjective. Recognition through transliteration is valid learning evidence but is not Arabic spelling mastery. Try closed-book recall before revealing script.

conceptRegistry.title: Talk about a dated announcement — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: With ish-shirka (the company), learn a'lanit (announced) and nazzilit (released). The feminine ending belongs to the company as grammatical subject. Do not add habitual bi- to these completed past forms. Imbaarih means yesterday relative to the speaker. A publication date is safer than calling an old story yesterday's news. Names and numerals are recognition-only.

conceptRegistry.title: Say when something happens — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Imta asks when, while feen asks where. Learn el-usbooʿ da (this week), ish-shahr da (this month), and baʿdeen (later) as time chunks. In colloquial Egyptian the demonstrative follows the noun here. A time phrase does not prove that a planned event happened. Use past a'lanit only for a completed announcement.

conceptRegistry.title: Plans are different from results — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use ha- with a small set of familiar verbs: ha'ra, I will read; haktib, I will write; hat'allim, I will learn. This replaces the habitual b-prefix; do not stack both prefixes. The spelling commonly joins ح to the verb. Il-usbooʿ el-gaay means next week. Future wording reports an intention or expectation, not a completed result or a guarantee. The future prefix can be written with حـ or هـ in colloquial spelling; this lesson uses هـ in its sentence examples.

conceptRegistry.title: Explain a simple reason — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Ashaan can mean because; today's examples put a full reason clause after it. Bass means but in our contrasts, though it can also mean only in other contexts. Kamaan adds too/also. Build short linked clauses rather than translating English word order mechanically. A reason for your personal choice is not a factual product-performance claim.

conceptRegistry.title: A scientist checks a result — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Compare biyraagi' (checks/is checking) with raaga' (checked), using a male researcher as the subject. Place the object after the verb: il-baahis biyraagi' in-nateega. The feminine result noun does not make the male subject's verb feminine. Mish ma'ruuf means unknown with a masculine subject; mish ma'ruufa with a feminine one. Do not infer medical usefulness from an early laboratory result.

conceptRegistry.title: Report what a company says — Egyptian sentence pattern
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use biy'uul with a male person and bit'uul with ish-shirka (the company). Hasab comes before the named source. Yimkin marks maybe; lissa mish works with nonverbal descriptions: lissa mish waadih, not clear yet. With verbs, negation may instead wrap ma-...-sh around the verb; do not generalise lissa mish to every construction. Reporting words and source names preserve uncertainty.

conceptRegistry.title: Szeretnék and kell as bounded chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use szeretnék + infinitive for I would like to do something: szeretnék tanulni. With a thing, learn the whole object chunk: egy eszközt szeretnék. Kell expresses necessity: Idő kell = Time is needed / I need time in context. It is not a conjugated equivalent of English I need. Do not put an object -t on idő in this frame. Contrast a polite wish with a need; Hungarian does not mark the speaker's gender.

conceptRegistry.title: Comparative -bb on learned adjectives; mint in a model frame
conceptRegistry.explanation: Learn olcsó → olcsóbb, gyors → gyorsabb, jó → jobb. Do not build the irregular jobb mechanically. The comparison target follows mint: Ez olcsóbb, mint az. In these singular adjective sentences there is no van. Más means different/another here, not more. Our comparisons of unnamed classroom tools are imagined; they do not establish a real model ranking.

conceptRegistry.title: Tud plus infinitive in limited ability frames
conceptRegistry.explanation: Tud + infinitive expresses ability: tud olvasni, can read. In Tudok egy fájlt olvasni, tudok marks I and olvasni stays infinitive. Do not add a second finite verb. Ability does not automatically mean authorization; ask Van engedély? separately. Learn Ellenőrizd a forrást, Check the source, as a bounded instruction, not a whole imperative paradigm. Elolvashatok egy fájlt? is a supported permission-request chunk, distinct from the ability frame tudok olvasni.

conceptRegistry.title: Mix prior forms without adding a new paradigm
conceptRegistry.explanation: Retrieve the previously learned need, wish, description and ability chunks. Szeretnék tanulni takes an infinitive; Idő kell has no object ending; Ez egy új eszköz has no van. A question about permission does not answer a question about safety. Do not learn a new paradigm today: identify which existing frame fits the communicative job.

conceptRegistry.title: A few high-frequency past-tense third-person chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: Bejelentette = announced it/the specified thing; kiadta = released it/the specified thing. Learn them with a named company and definite object, not as a full past-tense system. Tegnap means the day before the speaker's date; it is not permanently attached to a news article. A dated announcement and the moment you read it can be different days. Dates are recognition-only today.

conceptRegistry.title: Mikor and time expressions; past versus present context
conceptRegistry.explanation: Mikor asks when; hol asks where. Learn ezen a héten (this week), ebben a hónapban (this month) and később (later) as entire time chunks. They do not determine tense by themselves: a completed announcement still needs a past form. Hét means week here, but also seven in other contexts. Keep later distinct from an exact promised date.

conceptRegistry.title: Fog plus infinitive in fixed examples; date-relative caution
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use fog + infinitive for a limited future frame: A csapat tanulni fog. With I, use fogok: Tanulni fogok. The infinitive stays tanulni; the future auxiliary changes for the person. Hungarian also uses present forms for scheduled future events, but today's production uses these explicit chunks. A stated future plan is not evidence of a completed outcome.

conceptRegistry.title: Mert and de joining short clauses
conceptRegistry.explanation: Mert gives a reason; de introduces contrast. Build two short complete clauses: Idő kell, mert tanulok. Szeretnék tanulni, de ma dolgozom. Do not use mert when the second clause actually contradicts an expectation. Is normally follows the item it adds: Ma is tanulok, I learn today too. Keep this placement as a chunk for now.

conceptRegistry.title: Subject versus object recognition; short present and past contrast
conceptRegistry.explanation: The subject does the action; the object receives it. Compare A kutató ellenőriz and A kutató ellenőrzi az eredményt. Learn the definite-object chunk without memorising the conjugation table. The object ending appears on eredményt, not the researcher. Compare present ellenőrzi with past ellenőrizte. A check does not by itself mean a positive result.

conceptRegistry.title: Szerint and azt mondja fixed attribution chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: Szerint follows the source: az OpenAI szerint, according to OpenAI. Azt mondja, hogy introduces what someone says; learn the whole frame. Talán marks maybe. Még nem means not yet with a following verb/adjective; it is not the same as never. Attribution identifies a speaker, but does not prove that the claim is true.

conceptRegistry.title: Retrieve attribution, descriptive negation and temporal distinctions
conceptRegistry.explanation: Retrieve attribution without turning it into proof. Hasab (according to) names the source. Mesh negates a description, while lissa mesh means not yet before that description. To say an action has not happened yet, a different negative pattern is used; this is recognition-only, not a production target today. Kamaan means also; bass between two clauses means but. Use short familiar clauses and keep the uncertainty word when retelling.

conceptRegistry.title: Sequence markers with known verbs
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use el-awwal (first) and baʿdeen (then) to join familiar actions. Baʿd (after) and ʾabl (before) come before their noun phrase, unlike Hungarian postpositions. Baʿdeen can also mean later; the situation supplies the exact time. The b-prefix marks a present routine in these examples. The past forms aʿlanit and nazzilit have a feminine subject because company is feminine. Treat them as learned chunks, not a new full conjugation table.

conceptRegistry.title: If-conditions with a simple present or future response; no counterfactual lesson
conceptRegistry.explanation: Law introduces a possible condition. The response may use ha- for a future action: law ... hagarrab means if ... I will try. A description such as available is negated with mesh; it does not need the verbal ma-...-sh pattern. Imta asks when. Baʿd usbooʿ means in a week in this future setting; baʿdeen simply means later. do not infer a precise date from it. These are realistic conditions, not unreal past or counterfactual constructions.

conceptRegistry.title: I prefer as a chunk; adjective review
conceptRegistry.explanation: Bafaddal is a first-person preference chunk. A definite adjective follows a definite noun: the tool the simple. Kifaaya means enough; you can use it after a quantity or on its own. A feminine tool takes baseeta and ghaalya; a masculine model takes baseet and ghaali. Review the future ha- prefix in haktib and the conditional law. Preference is personal: never use the fictional dialogue to infer a real productʾs price or quality.

conceptRegistry.title: I do not understand, with speaker-gender agreement; explanation requests
conceptRegistry.explanation: A male speaker says ana mesh faahim; a female speaker says ana mesh faahma. These describe a state of understanding. For a request to one man, use ishrah; to one woman, ishrahi. Min fadlak and min fadlik likewise depend on the addressee, not the speaker. Birraaha can mean slowly or gently in context. Mathematically literal word-by-word translations are less useful than this natural request: explain it to me slowly. Use a clear example to repair understanding. For the supported reconstruction, learn babuss ʿala as one chunk meaning I look at. You may keep that chunk visible while producing the rest of the sentence.

conceptRegistry.title: Only, all and some in clear examples; distinguish only from but
conceptRegistry.explanation: Bass has two jobs. Between contrasting clauses it means but; after a limited item it can mean only: el-malaff da bass means only this file. Kull means all or every. Baʿd plus a definite plural gives some of the group; it is used in educated speech, while shwayyit is another everyday option meaning some/a few. Mesh kull means not all, which is different from none. Review agreement with feminine nateega and masculine ikhtibaar. scope words matter more than a dramatic headline.

conceptRegistry.title: In my opinion and why, with polite agreement chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: Fi raʾyi marks your opinion. Ana mowaafeʾ and ana mesh mowaafeʾ are agreement chunks for a male speaker; a female speaker uses mowaafʾa. Leeh asks why and ʿashaan supplies a reason. Agreeing with a person is not the same as independently verifying their claim. In conversation, disagree with a specific statement and give a reason. Keep lissa mesh before a descriptive predicate; do not omit lissa when the point is that evidence is not sufficient yet.

conceptRegistry.title: Mixed retrieval with Arabic-script and transliteration modes
conceptRegistry.explanation: Review three conversational moves: request an explanation, disagree politely, and propose a concrete example. Use the gender forms that fit the speaker and addressee; do not equate a transliterated answer with Arabic spelling mastery. In a nominal description, do not add a present-tense word for is. Fi raʾyi marks an opinion; leeh asks for the missing reason. If you need support, reveal one hint and then retry a different sentence before returning to the missed item.

conceptRegistry.title: Combine known sentence patterns; no new grammar
conceptRegistry.explanation: Combine familiar patterns rather than adding a new conjugation. A ʿinwaan is a headline or title; a haʾeeʾa is a fact; an iddiʿaaʾ is a claim or allegation; a daleel is evidence. In everyday speech you can also say the company says rather than using the more formal noun claim. The noun alone does not show whether something is true or false. Put ʾabl and baʿd before a noun, or use a supported before-I-answer chunk. Keep source and opinion markers when combining sentences.

conceptRegistry.title: Capstone in Egyptian dialect with script and transliteration
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use your known Egyptian chunks to make a small news brief. Keep a headline, the source date, one attributed statement and one limit. Fi raʾyi introduces your view; hasab introduces the sourceʾs position. Law supplies a practical condition if the source is unavailable. Choose masculine or feminine self-description deliberately. You may submit Arabic script or the consistent transliteration; these are different evidence of skill, so script accuracy must be tracked separately. Read the model only after trying your own version.

conceptRegistry.title: Retrieve attribution and temporal distinctions
conceptRegistry.explanation: Retrieve the difference between attribution and opinion: X szerint means according to X; szerintem marks your own opinion. Azt mondja introduces what someone says. Még nem means not yet and does not mean never. In a description, nem goes before the adjective; do not insert van into a third-person adjective sentence. Is normally follows the word it adds. Today introduces no new grammar. Read each pair, cover the Hungarian, then reconstruct only the short clause you can support.

conceptRegistry.title: Sequence markers with known verbs
conceptRegistry.explanation: Use először and aztán to order clauses with verbs you already know. Után and előtt follow the noun phrase: a munka után is after work; a teszt előtt is before the test. Do not place them before the noun as in English. Keep tense fixed within a small retelling: present for a routine, familiar past chunks for yesterday's fictional bulletin. Recognise ellenőrzöm as I check it and elolvasom as I read it through; the entire definite-conjugation system is not a production target.

conceptRegistry.title: Ha with a present-tense condition; no full conditional mood
conceptRegistry.explanation: Ha introduces a real or possible condition. Use familiar present-tense verbs in both halves; this is not the Hungarian conditional mood. Ha nem elérhető, később próbálom means if it is not available, I will try it later in this context. A comma separates the clauses. Mikor asks when; később is deliberately vague. A hét and a hónap mean the week and the month, while one week is egy hét. Keep uncertainty rather than inventing a date.

conceptRegistry.title: Jobban szeretem as a chunk and sufficient adjective practice
conceptRegistry.explanation: Jobban szeretem is a useful first-person chunk meaning I prefer. Learn the object with it: az egyszerű eszközt, the simple tool. Elég may mean enough by itself or stand before a quantity. Drága is expensive, while egyszerű is simple; these are judgments about the imagined tools, not claims about named products. Review a future chunk with fog plus infinitive, without memorising its entire paradigm. A következő feladat means the next task; the adjective stays before the noun.

conceptRegistry.title: Nem értem and please-explain chunks
conceptRegistry.explanation: Nem értem is a compact and useful repair phrase: I do not understand. Kérlek, magyarázd el means please explain it to someone you address informally. The verb and el separate in this imperative chunk; learn the whole request. Lassan is the adverb slowly, not the adjective slow. Egy példa is the subject form, but kérek egy példát uses an object form. Both are the same vocabulary family. Add mert for a reason and de for a contrast, keeping the request short.

conceptRegistry.title: Quantifier contrasts and explicit scope
conceptRegistry.explanation: Minden, néhány and numerals normally take singular nouns: minden fájl, néhány kutató, két teszt. Csak narrows the scope of the phrase that follows. Compare only this file with all files; neither implies anything about every user's access. In a negative sentence not every is different from no: nem minden fájl means not every file. Learn the contrast directly rather than building a large quantifier table. Keep teszt and eredmény separate: a test is a procedure, a result is what it produces.

conceptRegistry.title: Szerintem and miért conversation frames
conceptRegistry.explanation: Szerintem introduces your own view; Anna szerint attributes a view to Anna. Neither is evidence by itself. Miért asks why and mert gives a reason. Egyetértek is I agree, but the negative chunk is nem értek egyet: the verbal prefix separates in this learned pattern. Do not mechanically put nem before the whole positive word. A polite disagreement can name the particular point: I agree about the date, but not the conclusion. Today keep your production to one judgment and one reason.

conceptRegistry.title: Mixed retrieval focused on weakest concepts
conceptRegistry.explanation: This is retrieval, not a new paradigm. First try the three dialogue functions without a word bank: ask for explanation, express an opinion, and ask why. Then inspect any missed chunk. Distinguish értem from nem értem, and egyetértek from nem értek egyet. Request an example with példát, but name an example with példa. You can simplify a long sentence into two short ones and retain its meaning. Score independent production separately from reconstructed answers after seeing the model.

conceptRegistry.title: Combine known sentence patterns; no new grammar
conceptRegistry.explanation: No new grammar today. Combine familiar description, sequence and object chunks while introducing four news-literacy nouns. Cím can be a headline or title. Állítás is a claim, whether true or false; calling something a claim does not establish that it is false. Bizonyíték is evidence, and tény is a fact. Practise the object form in elolvasom a címet. Keep the noun forms supported; the main task is separating a title, a claim, and the evidence offered for it.

conceptRegistry.title: Capstone using known forms and source checking
conceptRegistry.explanation: This capstone combines known forms. Choose one source card, keep its date, and write a very short brief with a headline, one attributed statement and one limit. You may use two simple sentences instead of one long clause. Use ha for a condition, szerintem for your opinion and szerint for another source's position. Agreeing is not proof, and a well-written sentence is not proof that a product claim is true. A model brief is for comparison after your attempt; it is not a completed learner submission.
